world_behind.title: A reading already in progress
world_behind.text: Jacob told the colony he would read Isaiah to them (2 Ne. 6:4), and he has been reading since the middle of his second chapter. This chapter is Isaiah 50 entire. The break between it and what came before is a printer's decision, not Jacob's: his hearers heard the rescue promise of the previous verses and this accusation of abandonment in one breath.

world_behind.title: Debt and the loss of children
world_behind.text: The opening imagines two ways a household disappears: the wife dismissed with a written bill, the children handed to a creditor. Both were ordinary legal events in Israel, and neither is being denied here in principle. The question is narrower and sharper. Produce the document. Name the buyer.

world_behind.title: A colony that could ask this in earnest
world_behind.text: Some thirty years out of Jerusalem, on the far side of an ocean, split from half the family, this people had a live question about whether the covenant had lapsed at the shoreline. Isaiah wrote the words for exiles in Babylon. Jacob reads them to exiles who chose their exile.

world_behind.title: The taught ear
world_behind.text: Verses 4 and 5 describe a student, not an orator: an ear opened morning by morning, a tongue given rather than trained. Prophets in this record are usually shown receiving before speaking, and the image here is a daily lesson rather than a single call.

world_behind.title: Shame with legal weight
world_behind.text: Spitting and tearing out a man's beard were not merely rude in the ancient Near East; they were public sentences, ways of stripping a person of standing before witnesses. The servant does not describe pain in verse 6. He describes humiliation, which is the harder thing to volunteer for.

world_behind.title: Torches of your own making
world_behind.text: The last verse pictures people in the dark who strike their own sparks and walk by that light. Small fires were how anyone moved at night. The image is not of rebellion but of self-supply, and it is aimed at the same hearers who were just asked whether they walk in darkness with no light.

words.text: The word names a document, not a feeling. Israelite law required a written bill to end a marriage, and the bill was the wife's proof of release. God asks the abandoned people to bring theirs out. There is no such paper, which is the whole argument: separation without documentation is not divorce. It is desertion, and desertion is what the next clause pins on the deserters.

Twice in one verse, and the two uses are opposite ends of one skill. "The Lord God hath given me the tongue of the learned" (v. 4) is the gift of speech; "He waketh mine ear to hear as the learned" (v. 4) is the gift of hearing. The older sense is closer to taught than to scholarly. A taught tongue is downstream of a taught ear, and the verse puts them in that order.

words.text: Not confused. In older usage the word means publicly disgraced, put to shame in front of everyone watching. That is why it stands beside "ashamed" (v. 7) at the verse's other end, and why the flint face sits between them. The servant is not claiming he will avoid pain. He is claiming the shame will not stick.

The verb means to encircle, and the record has used it for the good version already, the compass that steered the family and the arms that hold up the faithful. Here people encircle themselves, and what they encircle themselves with is sparks. The ring is the same shape; everything depends on who draws it.

phrases.term: Have I put thee away, or have I cast thee off forever?
phrases.text: The reading opens with a question the KJV does not have. Isaiah 50:1 begins flatly, "Where is the bill of your mother's divorcement" (Isa. 50:1), and leaves the accusation unstated. Here the accusation is spoken first, in God's own mouth, before it is answered. Someone had said it. The added line lets the charge be heard before the evidence is demanded, which is a better order for people who have been carrying the charge silently.

phrases.term: when I came, there was no man
phrases.text: The KJV asks; this text tells. "Wherefore, when I came, was there no man?" (Isa. 50:2) becomes a plain report of an empty house, and the same change lands again at verse 9, where the KJV's "who is he that shall condemn me?" (Isa. 50:9) becomes "all they who shall condemn me" (v. 9). Rhetorical questions invite the hearer to supply an answer. Statements do not wait. Both variants push the passage from argument toward verdict.

cites.quote: all they who shall condemn me

spans.text: all they who shall condemn me

phrases.term: unto thee, O house of Israel
phrases.text: The KJV's servant speaks a word in season "to him that is weary" (Isa. 50:4), an unnamed individual. This reading names the whole house and speaks to it directly: "unto thee, O house of Israel" (v. 4), then "When ye are weary he waketh morning by morning" (v. 4). The weary man becomes a weary people, and Jacob is reading it to a weary people. Whether the difference is Isaiah's or the brass plates', the fit is exact.

cites.quote: unto thee, O house of Israel

spans.text: unto thee, O house of Israel

cites.quote: When ye are weary he waketh morning by morning

spans.text: When ye are weary he waketh morning by morning

phrases.term: I gave my back to the smiter
phrases.text: One letter apart from the KJV's "I gave my back to the smiters" (Isa. 50:6), and the singular changes what is pictured. A crowd becomes an appointed man doing his work. The verse is often read forward to the trial of Christ, and this record's own writers had read it that way already: Zenos, as Nephi transcribed him, wrote that "they spit upon him, and he suffereth it" (1 Ne. 19:9), the same scene from the other side, with the suffering man's consent named outright.

phrases.term: I will smite him with the strength of my mouth
phrases.text: The KJV's courtroom challenge ends open: "let him come near to me" (Isa. 50:8), and nothing follows. This reading finishes the sentence with a weapon. The servant who gave his back to the smiter now does some smiting, and what he strikes with is his mouth. Isaiah elsewhere promises a ruler who will "smite the earth with the rod of his mouth" (Isa. 11:4), a chapter this record will later quote in full. The added clause pulls that figure into the servant's own defense.

phrases.term: let him trust in the name of the Lord
phrases.text: This is the reading's most consequential absence. The KJV answers its own question in the same verse: whoever fears the Lord and walks in darkness should "let him trust in the name of the LORD, and stay upon his God" (Isa. 50:10). Here the verse stops at the question, and the darkness has no instruction attached to it. What follows instead is verse 11's picture of people lighting their own fires, which reads as the wrong answer to a question the text has deliberately left open. Jacob supplies the right one two chapters later, in his own voice.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: The papers nobody can produce
verses.text: The charge is desertion, and the reply is a demand for evidence. No bill exists; no creditor is named; the sale, if there was one, was made by the people themselves: "for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves" (v. 1). The verse does not deny the separation. It relocates the paperwork, and the hearer who came in feeling abandoned leaves the verse holding a receipt with his own signature on it.

cites.quote: for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves

spans.text: for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves

verses.label: v. 2–3
verses.title: An empty house, and a dried sea
verses.text: Two failures are reported, arrival and call, and neither found anyone home. Then the question that has been hanging since the first verse gets its answer in the form of a resume: the sea dried, the rivers made a wilderness, the heavens dressed in mourning. Absence was never weakness. "Is my hand shortened at all that it cannot redeem" (v. 2) is a question about capacity, and the exodus is the exhibit.

cites.quote: Is my hand shortened at all that it cannot redeem

spans.text: Is my hand shortened at all that it cannot redeem

verses.label: v. 4–5
verses.title: Morning by morning
verses.text: The voice changes without warning. A servant speaks, and his credentials are entirely receptive: a given tongue, an opened ear, a daily waking. Verse 5 adds the only thing he claims to have done himself, which is not to have turned back. Everything else on his side of the ledger was handed to him, which makes the obedience of the next verse harder rather than easier to read as heroism.

verses.label: v. 6
verses.title: The three things given
verses.text: Back, cheeks, face. Each is volunteered in the same grammar, and the verse's power is in what it does not say: no protest is recorded, no explanation offered, no outcome promised. The reader who knows where this leads supplies the rest; Jacob's hearers had been told four verses into chapter 6 that their God would be scourged and crucified, so they were reading this with the ending already in hand.

verses.label: v. 7–8
verses.title: A face like stone, and a court in session
verses.text: The servant's confidence arrives immediately after the humiliation, which is the chapter's most surprising seam. He is not confounded, not ashamed, and he is not alone: "And the Lord is near, and he justifieth me" (v. 8). What follows is a challenge to any accuser to stand up in the same room. The man who would not turn his face from spitting also will not turn it from a fight.

cites.quote: And the Lord is near, and he justifieth me

spans.text: And the Lord is near, and he justifieth me

verses.label: v. 9
verses.title: Moths finish the accusers
verses.text: The threat is not that opponents will be struck down but that they will wear out. Garments do not resist moths; they simply stop being garments. Set against the flint of verse 7, the contrast is between something that hardens and something that quietly comes apart, and time does the work in both directions.

verses.label: v. 10–11
verses.title: Two ways to be in the dark
verses.text: The last two verses sort the hearers. One walks in darkness fearing the Lord and obeying his servant's voice, and this reading gives that person no lamp at all, only the question. The other kindles a fire, encircles himself with sparks, and is told to walk in that light for as long as it lasts. The judgment is not a lightning bolt; it is being left with exactly the light you made. "Ye shall lie down in sorrow" (v. 11) is where the reading stops.

cites.quote: Ye shall lie down in sorrow

spans.text: Ye shall lie down in sorrow

chapter.title: The reading answers the colony's actual question
chapter.text: Jacob's people are not asking whether God can save. They are asking whether he still wants them, which is what an ocean and a broken family put in a person's mouth. Isaiah 50 is the chapter in which that question is stated out loud and refused, and Jacob puts it in front of them before he preaches a word of his own.

chapter.title: The seam with the previous chapter is invisible by design
chapter.text: Chapter 6 ended with God promising to contend with those who contend with his people. Verse 8 here has the servant asking who will contend with him. Read as one reading, which is how it was delivered, the promise and the challenge belong to the same voice inside a dozen verses.

chapter.title: The variants run one direction
chapter.text: Questions become statements (v. 2, v. 9), an unnamed weary man becomes the house of Israel (v. 4), an open-ended challenge gains a weapon (v. 8). Each change makes the text less suggestive and more declarative. The pattern matches what the record's other Isaiah blocks do to their source, and it is worth noticing that the accusation itself gets the same treatment: it is added, not softened.

chapter.title: One absence outweighs the additions
chapter.text: Dropping the KJV's trust clause at verse 10 leaves the fearing, obeying, darkness-walking hearer without a remedy inside the chapter. That looks like a loss until the sermon is read whole. Jacob has arranged his reading so that the unanswered verse hands directly into his own great chapter on deliverance, where the remedy fills forty verses instead of one clause.

chapter.title: The servant is not introduced
chapter.text: No name, no formula, no "thus saith" before the voice changes at verse 4. Some readers take the speaker to be Isaiah himself describing a prophet's lot; the record's own reading is fixed by what Jacob said before he opened the text, and by Abinadi and others afterward. The chapter itself leaves the identification to be made from outside it, which is part of why it needed a sermon around it.

chapter.title: Judgment closes the reading, as it did before
chapter.text: The last Isaiah block in this record ended by sorting its hearers, and so does this one. The habit is worth naming: these readings do not end in comfort even when comfort is their subject, because the comfort is conditional and the last verse is where the condition gets stated.

chapter.title: A short chapter carrying the unit's hinge
chapter.text: Eleven verses sit between Jacob's opening argument and the long reading that follows, and they change the sermon's subject from what God will do for Israel to what God's servant will suffer. Everything after this in the unit assumes that turn has been made.

applications.title: Ask for the paperwork
applications.text: When the feeling of having been dropped by God shows up, treat it the way this verse does. Name the document. What actually happened, when, and who left? Most of the time the honest answer changes the accusation into an inventory, and an inventory can be worked through.

applications.title: Check whether anyone was home
applications.text: The verse reports an arrival that found no one and a call that got no answer. Before concluding that heaven went silent, audit the other side of the appointment: the prayers begun and abandoned, the impressions filed away. Silence has two possible addresses.

applications.title: Train the ear first
applications.text: The servant's tongue is given after his ear is opened, and the opening happens daily. Pick one fixed morning slot this week, short and unmissable, and spend it listening rather than asking. Speech in season is a downstream benefit; the schedule is the practice.

applications.title: Decide what you will not turn from
applications.text: The servant's single active verb is refusing to turn back. Name in advance the one commitment you will keep when it stops being admired, and write down what keeping it will probably cost. Deciding under pressure is how good people discover they never decided.

applications.title: Let the moths do their work
applications.text: Not every accuser needs answering. Identify one criticism you have been drafting replies to in your head and consciously hand it to time. If it is false, it will wear out. Your job in the meantime is the flint face, not the rebuttal.

applications.title: Count your own sparks
applications.text: List the small fires you light to get through a dark stretch: distraction, overwork, someone else's approval. They do give light, which is why the verse grants it. Then ask how long each one burns, and what you will be lying down in when it goes out.

questions.text: What exactly am I accusing God of having done, and would I put it in writing with dates?
Where in the last month did God arrive or call, and was there a man to answer?
Is my tongue ahead of my ear right now, and which one have I been training?
Which humiliation would I accept for someone else's sake, and where is my actual limit?
Whose condemnation of me am I still carrying, and what would change if I let it wear out?
When I walk in darkness fearing the Lord, what do I reach for first, and is it a spark of my own striking?
